title: Fire from Heaven, and the Mantle Falls
subtitle: 2 Kings 1
description: Elijah is taken up in the whirlwind, and Elisha takes up the mantle, the Jordan, and the work.
paragraphs: The two books of Kings are one book in the Hebrew text, and this half opens without a pause, days after Ahab's death, with the kingdom already coming apart at its edges: “After the death of Ahab, Moab rebelled against Israel.” In Samaria, Ahab's son Ahaziah fell through the lattice of his upper room and lay badly hurt, and the injured king sent messengers to Ekron, to a Philistine god with a name the text gives as Baal-zebub, to ask whether he would recover. Elijah the Tishbite met the embassy on the road, sent by an angel, with a question that is the whole scene: “Is it because there is no God in Israel that you are on your way to inquire of Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron?” And with the question came the sentence: “You will not get up from the bed on which you are lying. You will surely die.” The messengers turned back without ever reaching Ekron, and when the king demanded a description of the man who had stopped them, they said: “He was a hairy man,” “with a leather belt around his waist.” Ahaziah knew the description the way all Israel knew it. “It was Elijah the Tishbite,” said the king.

So the king sent soldiers to fetch the prophet, a captain with fifty men, who found Elijah sitting on top of a hill and ordered him down in the king's name. Elijah answered: “If I am a man of God, may fire come down from heaven and consume you and your fifty men.” Fire fell, and it did. A second captain came with the same order and more haste in it, and the fire of God fell again. The third captain climbed the hill on his knees and begged for his life: “Man of God, may my life and the lives of these fifty servants of yours please be precious in your sight.” “But now may my life be precious in your sight.” The angel told Elijah to go down with him and not be afraid, and Elijah stood before the king and said the sentence to his face. Ahaziah died as the word had said, and because he had no son, his brother Jehoram took the throne. The fire scenes are told without comment, twice repeated and once refused, and the text lets the difference between the captains speak for itself.

Then the book turns to the old prophet's last journey, and it is walked at a companion's pace. Elijah and Elisha set out from Gilgal, and three times, at Bethel, at Jericho, and at the Jordan, Elijah tried to release his servant from following: “Please stay here, for the LORD has sent me on to Bethel.” Three times Elisha refused with the same oath: “As surely as the LORD lives and as you yourself live, I will not leave you.” At each stop the sons of the prophets came out to Elisha with the news everyone somehow knew: “Do you know that the LORD will take your master away from you today?” “Yes, I know,” he replied. “Do not speak of it.” At the Jordan, Elijah rolled up his cloak and struck the water, and it parted, and the two crossed on dry ground, fifty of the sons of the prophets watching from a distance. On the far side, Elijah offered one last gift: “Tell me, what can I do for you before I am taken away from you?” Elisha asked for the heir's share: “Please, let me inherit a double portion of your spirit”. Elijah answered: “You have requested a difficult thing,” said Elijah. “Nevertheless, if you see me as I am taken from you, it will be yours. But if not, then it will not be so.”

What Elisha saw was fire again, but fire of another kind: “suddenly a chariot of fire with horses of fire appeared and separated the two of them, and Elijah went up into heaven in a whirlwind.” Elisha cried out: “My father, my father, the chariots and horsemen of Israel!” and tore his clothes. Then he picked up the cloak that had fallen from Elijah and stood on the bank of the Jordan and struck the water with it, asking: “Where now is the LORD, the God of Elijah?” The water parted for him as it had for his master, and the watching prophets read the sign correctly: “The spirit of Elijah rests on Elisha.” They still begged to send fifty men searching the mountains and valleys in case the Spirit had set Elijah down somewhere, and when Elisha finally yielded to their embarrassment and let them go, they searched three days and found nothing. His answer when they returned was gentle by his standards: “Didn’t I tell you not to go?”

Elisha's first works as the heir were acts of repair. At Jericho the men of the city brought him their problem, good land poisoned by bad water, and he threw salt from a new bowl into the spring and spoke the word: “I have healed this water. No longer will it cause death or unfruitfulness.” The text adds that the water has been healthy to this day. Then comes the scene this episode will not soften. On the road up to Bethel, a group of boys came out of the city jeering at the prophet: “Go up, you baldhead! Go up, you baldhead!” Elisha turned, looked at them, “and called down a curse on them in the name of the LORD. Suddenly two female bears came out of the woods and mauled forty-two of the boys.” The book records it in three sentences and moves on to Mount Carmel and Samaria without explanation or apology, and this retelling leaves it where the book leaves it: the strange, severe first sign that the mantle had passed to a man through whom the word of the LORD acted, for healing and for judgment alike.

title: Water in the Desert
subtitle: 2 Kings 3
description: Three kings march against Moab, run out of water, and get a word about ditches.
paragraphs: Elisha's first public work was done in a war he wanted no part of. Jehoram, Ahab's son, now reigned in Samaria. He was not his father and mother, the text is careful to say: he removed the sacred pillar of Baal Ahab had made. “Nevertheless, he clung to the sins that Jeroboam son of Nebat had caused Israel to commit; he did not turn away from them.” Moab had paid Israel a yearly tribute of a hundred thousand lambs and the wool of a hundred thousand rams, and with Ahab dead, Moab stopped paying. Jehoram mobilized Israel and called on Judah to join the campaign, and Jehoshaphat answered with the old alliance in full: “I am as you are, my people are your people, and my horses are your horses”. The road Jehoram chose went around by the Desert of Edom, seven days of marching with the king of Edom's forces added, and at the end of it there was no water, for the army or for the animals dying around them.

Jehoram read the disaster as a trap: he cried out, “Alas,” said the king of Israel, “for the LORD has summoned these three kings to deliver them into the hand of Moab!” Jehoshaphat asked the question he always asked, whether a prophet of the LORD was anywhere near, and one of Jehoram's own servants knew the answer: “Elisha son of Shaphat is here. He used to pour water on the hands of Elijah.” Jehoshaphat affirmed: “The word of the LORD is with him.” So three kings went down to a prophet's camp to ask for help, and Elisha greeted the king of Israel with open contempt: “What have we to do with each other? Go to the prophets of your father and of your mother!” Only Jehoshaphat's presence bought Jehoram an answer at all: “As surely as the LORD of Hosts lives, before whom I stand, were it not for my regard for the presence of Jehoshaphat king of Judah, I would not look at you or acknowledge you.” Then the prophet asked for music, a harpist, and while the harpist played, the hand of the LORD came on him.

The word he spoke was strange and practical: “Dig this valley full of ditches.” Rain would not do this the ordinary way. “You will not see wind or rain, but the valley will be filled with water, and you will drink”, and your cattle and your animals with you. “This is a simple matter in the sight of the LORD”, Elisha said, “and He will also deliver the Moabites into your hand.” The kings were told to press the victory hard: every fortified city attacked, every good tree cut down, every spring stopped, every good field ruined with stones. The next morning, at the hour of the morning sacrifice, water flowed into the valley from the direction of Edom and filled the land. Across the border, the Moabites had mustered everyone who could bear arms and were watching at dawn. The sun shone on the water and it looked red to them, red as blood, and they read it as their deliverance: “This is blood!” they exclaimed. “The kings have clashed swords and slaughtered one another. Now to the plunder, Moab!” They charged a camp that was waiting for them, and Israel rose up and struck them down and invaded Moab, doing everything the word had listed, city by city, field by field, spring by spring, until only Kir-haraseth stood, ringed by slingers.

Then the episode ends with the scene it will not explain. Mesha, king of Moab, tried to break through to the king of Edom with seven hundred swordsmen and failed, and from the wall of his last city, in sight of the armies below, “he took his firstborn son, who was to succeed him, and offered him as a burnt offering on the city wall.” Whatever the watchers below made of it, the text records the effect in one flat sentence: “there was great fury against the Israelites, so they withdrew and returned to their own land.” The victory the LORD had given stopped at that wall. The book does not say what the fury was, whose it was, or what the kings thought as they marched home, and this retelling leaves the silence exactly where the book leaves it: water in a dry valley, given freely, and a war that ended in a way nobody in it had planned.

title: Oil, Bread, and a Son Raised
subtitle: 2 Kings 4
description: A widow's oil, a Shunammite's son, poison drawn from a pot, and bread that outlasts the count.
paragraphs: Between the wars, the book follows Elisha into kitchens and sickrooms, and the first is a widow's. Her husband, one of the sons of the prophets, was dead, and his creditor was coming to take her two sons as slaves for the debt. She cried out to Elisha: “Your servant, my husband, is dead, and you know that your servant feared the LORD.” All she had left in the house, she told him, was one thing: “Your servant has nothing in the house but a jar of oil.” Elisha's answer built the miracle out of her neighbors: “borrow empty jars from all your neighbors. Do not gather just a few.” Then she was to shut the door behind her and her sons and pour. The oil flowed jar to jar until the last borrowed vessel was full. Her son said, “There are no more jars.” Then the oil stopped, not before. Elisha's instruction closed the scene like a ledger balanced: “Go, sell the oil, and pay your debt. Then you and your sons can live on the remainder.” A debt cancelled, two boys free, and a household living on what a single jar became behind a shut door.

The second household is in Shunem, where a prominent woman persuaded the passing prophet to stop for meals, then persuaded her husband to build him a small upstairs room, a bed, a table, a chair, a lamp. Elisha wanted to repay her and offered the only currency a prophet at court might have, a word spoken for her to the king or the commander of the army. Her answer is one of the quietest lines in the book: “I have a home among my own people,” she replied. She asked for nothing. It was Gehazi, the servant, who named the absence in her life: she had no son, and her husband was old. Elisha called her to the doorway and made the promise she had not dared to request: “At this time next year, you will hold a son in your arms.” Her response was not joy but fear of hope itself: “Do not lie to your maidservant, O man of God.” She conceived, and the son was born at the time appointed, just as Elisha had told her.

The child grew, and one day in the harvest field he cried out to his father, “My head! My head!” and was carried to his mother, and sat on her lap until noon, and died. What the mother did next is the spine of the story. She laid the boy on the prophet's bed, shut the door, saddled a donkey, and refused every question, including her husband's, with one sentence: “Everything is all right.” She rode to Mount Carmel and would not answer Gehazi's questions either, the same sentence again, until she reached Elisha and clung to his feet. When Gehazi moved to push her away, Elisha stopped him: “Leave her alone, for her soul is in deep distress, and the LORD has hidden it from me and has not told me.” Her words then were an accusation aimed at the gift itself: “Did I ask you for a son, my lord?” She reminded him she had begged, “Do not deceive me?” Elisha sent Gehazi ahead with his staff to lay on the boy's face, an errand of haste, but the mother would not be separated from the prophet himself, and she used Elisha's own oath, the one he had sworn at the Jordan: “As surely as the LORD lives and as you yourself live, I will not leave you.” So he got up and followed her. The staff accomplished nothing. Gehazi met them with the report: “The boy has not awakened.”

In the upper room, behind a closed door, Elisha prayed, then stretched himself over the child, mouth to mouth, eye to eye, hand to hand, until the boy's body grew warm. He paced the room, returned, stretched himself out again, and the boy sneezed seven times and opened his eyes. Elisha's whole commission to the mother was three words: “Pick up your son.” She fell at his feet, bowed to the ground, picked up her son, and went out.

The episode closes with two smaller works at the table. At Gilgal, in a famine, one of the sons of the prophets gathered wild gourds into the communal stew without knowing what they were, and the first taste brought the cry: “There is death in the pot, O man of God!” Elisha threw in flour, and there was nothing harmful in the pot. Then a man arrived from Baal-shalishah with twenty loaves of barley bread, the first ripe grain, and Elisha ordered it set before a hundred men. His servant protested the arithmetic, and Elisha answered with the word that governed the meal: “They will eat and have some left over.” They ate, and they had some left over, according to the word of the LORD. Oil that fills a street of jars, a son restored behind a shut door, poison drawn out of a pot, bread that outlasts the count: the book is building its portrait of the heir of Elijah one household at a time.

title: Naaman and Gehazi
subtitle: 2 Kings 5
description: Aram's commander is healed in the Jordan, and the prophet's servant takes the disease he tried to sell.
paragraphs: The healing of Naaman begins with the book's most unlikely herald: a captured Israelite girl, serving in the house of Aram's great commander. Naaman was a mighty man of valor, honored by his king because through him the LORD had given victory to Aram, “but he was a leper.” The girl, taken in a raid, said to her mistress: “If only my master would go to the prophet who is in Samaria, he would cure him of his leprosy.” The word climbed from a servant's mouth to a king's ear, and Naaman traveled south with a royal letter and a fortune: ten talents of silver, six thousand shekels of gold, ten sets of clothing. But the letter was addressed to the wrong man. It asked the king of Israel to cure the leprosy, and Jehoram read it as a trap and tore his clothes: “Am I God, killing and giving life, that this man expects me to cure a leper?” “Surely you can see that he is seeking a quarrel with me!” Elisha heard of the torn clothes and sent the correction: “Why have you torn your clothes? Please let the man come to me, and he will know that there is a prophet in Israel.”

So Naaman's cavalcade stopped at the door of Elisha's house, and the prophet did not come out. He sent a messenger with the whole prescription: “Go and wash yourself seven times in the Jordan, and your flesh will be restored, and you will be clean.” Naaman went away angry, and his complaint is the sound of a great man insulted by a small instruction: “I thought that he would surely come out, stand and call on the name of the LORD his God, and wave his hand over the spot to cure my leprosy.” The rivers of home were better water anyway: “Are not the Abanah and Pharpar, the rivers of Damascus, better than all the waters of Israel? Could I not have washed in them and been cleansed?” He turned for home in a rage, and his own servants talked him down with the logic of the humble: “My father, if the prophet had told you to do some great thing, would you not have done it?” How much more, then, when the word was only, “Wash and be cleansed”. Naaman went down into the Jordan and dipped seven times, “and his flesh was restored and became like that of a little child, and he was clean.”

He returned with all his attendants to stand before the prophet he had not been deemed worth coming out for, and made the confession the whole episode was built to hold: “Now I know for sure that there is no God in all the earth except in Israel.” Then he pressed his fortune on Elisha as a gift, and Elisha refused it with an oath: “As surely as the LORD lives, before whom I stand, I will not accept it.” The healing of God was not for sale, not even to a grateful general. Naaman asked instead for something stranger than gold: “please let me, your servant, be given as much soil as a pair of mules can carry.” Israelite earth to worship on in Damascus, because, he said, “your servant will never again make a burnt offering or a sacrifice to any other god but the LORD.” And he made one honest confession of the compromise waiting for him at home, that when his king leaned on his arm in the temple of Rimmon, he would have to bow too, and he asked pardon for it in advance: “may the LORD forgive your servant this one thing”. Elisha let him go in peace.

Then the episode turns, and the servant who carried the prophet's errands ran after the chariot for the prophet's price. Gehazi had watched the fortune refused and could not bear it: “my master has spared this Aramean, Naaman, by not accepting what he brought.” He caught up with Naaman and told a lie built entirely out of the prophet's world: “Everything is all right,” Gehazi replied, the very words the Shunammite had used in truth, now borrowed for a fraud. His master had sent him, he said: “Look, two young men from the sons of the prophets have just now come to me from the hill country of Ephraim. Please give them a talent of silver and two sets of clothing.” Naaman, generous as the healed are, insisted: “Please, take two talents.” Gehazi took them, hid them in the house, dismissed the servants, and stood before Elisha with a clear face and a small answer: “Your servant did not go anywhere,” he replied. Elisha's questions stripped the lie in two strokes: “Did not my spirit go with you when the man got down from his chariot to meet you?” “Is this the time to accept money and clothing, olive groves and vineyards, sheep and oxen, menservants and maidservants?” The sentence matched the theft to its source: “the leprosy of Naaman will cling to you and your descendants forever!” Gehazi went out from his master's presence leprous, white as snow: the disease the Jordan had washed off the foreigner now settled on the prophet's own servant, who had tried to sell what God had given away.

title: The Siege of Samaria
subtitle: 2 Kings 6
description: Blind raiders are feasted, a starving city hears tomorrow's prices, and four lepers find an empty camp.
paragraphs: Elisha's war ministry opened with a borrowed axe. The sons of the prophets were cutting timber at the Jordan for a larger dwelling when one man's iron axe head flew off into the water, and his cry was about the debt, not the tool: “it was borrowed!” Elisha cut a stick, threw it where the iron had sunk, and the iron floated, and the man took it out. Then the book scales the same gift up to armies. Aram was raiding Israel, and every ambush the king of Aram planned, Elisha reported to Israel's king in advance: “Be careful not to pass by this place, for the Arameans are going down there.” Aram's king, enraged, demanded to know which of his own servants was the traitor, and the answer named the real problem: “Elisha, the prophet in Israel, tells the king of Israel the very words you speak in your bedroom.” So a great army came by night to Dothan to capture one prophet. Elisha's servant went out at dawn, saw horses and chariots ringing the city, and cried: “Oh, my master, what are we to do?” Elisha answered: “Do not be afraid,” “for those who are with us are more than those who are with them.” Then he prayed, “O LORD, please open his eyes that he may see.” And the young man saw “the hills were full of horses and chariots of fire all around Elisha.” Elisha's second prayer struck the Arameans blind, and the prophet walked out and offered to lead them to the man they were seeking, and led them ten miles into Samaria itself before their eyes were opened. Israel's king, looking at an army delivered into his capital, asked twice: “My father, shall I kill them? Shall I kill them?” Elisha forbade it: “Would you kill those you have captured with your own sword or bow? Set food and water before them, that they may eat and drink and then return to their master.” The king feasted them and sent them home. “And the Aramean raiders did not come into the land of Israel again.”

Some time later the raids became a siege, and the story darkens past anything in the book so far. Ben-hadad brought his entire army against Samaria and shut it in until the famine priced a donkey's head at eighty shekels of silver and a quarter cab of dove's dung at five. As the king walked the wall, a woman cried out: “Help me, my lord the king!” His answer was a starving man's theology: “If the LORD does not help you, where can I find help for you? From the threshing floor or the winepress?” Then she told him her matter. Another woman had proposed eating her son one day and the other's the next: “Give up your son, that we may eat him, and tomorrow we will eat my son.” “So we boiled my son and ate him,” she said, and on the second day the other woman had hidden her child: “But she had hidden her son.” The king tore his clothes, and the people watching saw that under them, against his skin, he was already wearing sackcloth. His grief turned on the prophet: “May God punish me, and ever so severely, if the head of Elisha son of Shaphat remains on his shoulders through this day!” Elisha, sitting with the elders in his house, knew the executioner was coming before the messenger arrived: “Do you see how this murderer has sent someone to cut off my head?” Then the king himself arrived with the despair that had replaced his oath: “This calamity is from the LORD. Why should I wait for the LORD any longer?”

Elisha's answer was a price list for the next morning: “About this time tomorrow at the gate of Samaria, a seah of fine flour will sell for a shekel, and two seahs of barley will sell for a shekel.” The officer on whose arm the king leaned answered for every reasonable person in the city: “Look, even if the LORD were to make windows in heaven, could this really happen?” Elisha's reply fixed the man's place in the story: “You will see it with your own eyes,” “but you will not eat any of it.”

That night the deliverance was discovered by the four hungriest men in Samaria, lepers camped at the gate because the city could not take them in. Their reasoning was the siege's arithmetic stripped bare: “Why just sit here until we die?” In the city, famine; at the gate, death; in the Aramean camp, a chance: “If they let us live, we will live; if they kill us, we will die.” They went at twilight and found the camp empty, because the LORD had made the Arameans hear the sound of chariots and horses and a great army, and the whole force had fled believing “the king of Israel must have hired the kings of the Hittites and Egyptians to attack us.” The lepers ate and drank in one tent, carried off silver and gold and clothing and hid them, entered a second tent and did the same, and then conscience caught up with appetite: “We are not doing what is right. Today is a day of good news.” “If we are silent and wait until morning light, our sin will overtake us.” They called the news up to the gatekeepers: “We went to the Aramean camp and no one was there”, “only tethered horses and donkeys, and the tents were intact.”

The king suspected a trap and sent scouts, who followed a road littered with discarded clothing and equipment all the way to the Jordan. Then the city poured out and plundered the camp, and by the gate the prices Elisha had named were the prices in the market, a seah of fine flour for a shekel, two seahs of barley for a shekel, according to the word of the LORD. The officer on whose arm the king leaned had been put in charge of that gate. He saw it all, exactly as promised. “The people trampled him in the gateway, and he died.”

title: The Shunammite's Land, and Hazael
subtitle: 2 Kings 8
description: The Shunammite gets her land back from the king, and Elisha weeps over the king Hazael will become.
paragraphs: The episode opens with a story told inside the story, and its timing is the point. Before a seven-year famine, Elisha had warned the Shunammite woman to leave the land: “Arise, you and your household; go and live as a foreigner wherever you can. For the LORD has decreed that a seven-year famine will come to the land.” She had obeyed, lived seven years among the Philistines, and came back to find her house and land in other hands, so she went to appeal to the king. The king, at that very hour, was asking Gehazi to relate all the great things Elisha had done, and Gehazi was in the middle of the story of the boy restored to life when the woman herself walked in to make her appeal. Gehazi's introduction is the book's own stage direction: “My lord the king, this is the woman, and this is the son Elisha restored to life.” The king questioned her, she confirmed the account, and he appointed an officer with a restitution order that went past the land itself: “Restore all that was hers, along with all the proceeds of the field from the day that she left the country until now.” Seven years of harvests she never planted, repaid. The woman who once asked for nothing and said she had a home among her own people received, in the king's court, the full value of the years she had spent as a foreigner for obeying a prophet's warning.

Then Elisha went to Damascus, into the capital of Israel's enemy, and the errand there ran the opposite direction. Ben-hadad, king of Aram, lay sick, and hearing the man of God had come, he sent Hazael, his courtier, with forty camel loads of gifts and one question: “Will I recover from this illness?” Elisha's answer was a riddle with a knife inside it: “You will surely recover.” “But the LORD has shown me that in fact he will die.” Then the prophet did something stranger than the riddle. He fixed his gaze on Hazael and held it until the courtier grew uncomfortable, and then the man of God wept. Hazael asked why, and Elisha told him what he saw coming, not for Ben-hadad but from Hazael himself: “Because I know the evil you will do to the Israelites,” Elisha replied. “You will set fire to their fortresses, kill their young men with the sword, dash their little ones to pieces, and rip open their pregnant women.” Hazael protested with the humility of a man who has not yet done it: “But how could your servant, a mere dog, do such a monstrous thing?” And Elisha answered: “The LORD has shown me that you will be king over Aram.” Hazael went back to his master and delivered the safe half of the message: “He told me that you would surely recover.” The next day he took a thick cloth, dipped it in water, spread it over the sleeping king's face, and took the throne.

The chapter's second half drops south to Judah, and the tone darkens into ledgers. Jehoram of Judah had married a daughter of Ahab, and he walked in the ways of the house of Ahab in Jerusalem. The book keeps one light burning through the record: “the LORD was unwilling to destroy Judah”, for David's sake, because of the promised lamp. Under Jehoram, Edom broke free of Judah and set up its own king, and Libnah followed. His son Ahaziah, whose mother was Athaliah, Omri's granddaughter, also walked in the ways of the house of Ahab, “for he was a son-in-law of the house of Ahab.” Ahaziah went north with Joram of Israel to fight Hazael at Ramoth-gilead, the new king of Aram already drawing Israelite blood, and Joram was wounded and carried back to Jezreel to recover. Ahaziah went down to Jezreel to visit him, an act of family loyalty between two kings of Ahab's house, and the book closes the chapter there, with both kings in one city and Elisha's anointing errand about to be sent. The stage is set so precisely because the next episode needs no setup at all.

title: Jehu's Revolt
subtitle: 2 Kings 9
description: Jehu is anointed in secret and drives to Jezreel, where two kings and a queen meet Elijah's word.
paragraphs: The revolt begins in an inner room, with a flask of oil and an order to run. Elisha summoned one of the sons of the prophets and sent him to Ramoth-gilead, where Israel's army was holding the line against Hazael and its commander, Jehu, sat with his fellow officers. The young prophet was to take Jehu aside, pour the oil on his head, deliver the commission, and flee: “I anoint you king over Israel.” The commission he carried was longer than the anointing line. Jehu was to strike down the house of Ahab, “you are to strike down the house of your master Ahab, so that I may avenge the blood of My servants the prophets”, and the blood of all the servants of the LORD shed by Jezebel's hand. The house of Ahab would be made like the houses of Jeroboam and Baasha before it, and its queen's end was named in advance: “on the plot of ground at Jezreel the dogs will devour Jezebel, and there will be no one to bury her.” The young prophet poured the oil and declared, “I anoint you king over the LORD’s people Israel.” Then he opened the door and ran, exactly as instructed. Jehu's fellow officers, told that a madman had come and gone, demanded the message, and when Jehu repeated it, each man stripped off his garment and laid it under Jehu's feet on the bare steps, blew the ram's horn, and proclaimed: “Jehu is king!”

Jehu's first act as king was to seal the camp: no one was to escape to carry the news to Jezreel, where Joram lay recovering from his wounds with Ahaziah of Judah visiting at his side. Then he drove. The watchman on Jezreel's tower saw the company coming and sent a rider to ask the formal question, “Have you come in peace?” Jehu's answer absorbed the messenger into the revolt: “What do you know about peace?” “Fall in behind me.” A second rider got the same words and the same fate, and the watchman, studying the distant chariot, named the driver by his driving: “he is driving like a madman!” Joram and Ahaziah came out to meet him, each in his own chariot, and they met Jehu on the one piece of ground in Israel where this confrontation had to happen: the property of Naboth the Jezreelite, the vineyard Ahab had taken by murder. Joram asked his own question: “Have you come in peace, Jehu?” Jehu answered: “How can there be peace,” “as long as the idolatry and witchcraft of your mother Jezebel abound?” Joram reined around and fled, shouting the alarm to his nephew: “Treachery, Ahaziah!” Jehu's arrow caught him between the shoulders and pierced his heart, and he slumped in his chariot. Jehu ordered the body thrown onto Naboth's plot, and quoted the oracle Elijah had spoken over that field years before: “As surely as I saw the blood of Naboth and the blood of his sons yesterday, declares the LORD, so will I repay you on this plot of ground, declares the LORD.” Ahaziah fled toward Beth-haggan, was shot in his chariot on the Ascent of Gur, and died at Megiddo, and his servants carried him home to burial in Jerusalem.

Then Jehu entered Jezreel, and the queen mother was waiting for him at a window, her eyes painted, her head adorned. Jezebel's last words were a taunt aimed at the history of coups like his: “Have you come in peace, O Zimri, murderer of your master?” Zimri had reigned seven days. Jehu ignored the taunt and addressed the palace staff instead: “Who is on my side? Who?” Two or three eunuchs looked down, and he gave the order: “Throw her down!” Her blood splattered the wall and the horses, and they trampled her underfoot. Jehu went inside and ate and drank, and only then remembered the forms: “Take care of this cursed woman,” he said, “and bury her, for she was the daughter of a king.” But when they went out to bury her, they found nothing left but her skull, her feet, and the palms of her hands. Jehu's verdict on the discovery closes the episode and reaches back two books for its authority: “On the plot of ground at Jezreel the dogs will devour the flesh of Jezebel.” “Jezebel’s body will lie like dung in the field on the plot of ground at Jezreel, so that no one can say: This is Jezebel.” The word Elijah had spoken at Naboth's vineyard, the word that had hung over the house of Ahab through the whole of 1 Kings, was now fully paid, and the man who collected it was just getting started.

title: The Purge, and the Hidden Child
subtitle: 2 Kings 10
description: Jehu finishes Ahab's house and Baal's temple, and in Jerusalem a child survives a queen's purge.
paragraphs: Jehu's purge was conducted by letter before it was conducted by sword. Ahab had seventy sons in Samaria, guarded by the city's officials and elders, and Jehu wrote to their guardians with a challenge dressed as a choice: “select the best and most worthy son of your master, set him on his father’s throne, and fight for your master’s house.” The men who received it did the arithmetic of the last chapter: “If two kings could not stand against him, how can we?” They surrendered in writing: “We are your servants, and we will do whatever you say. We will not make anyone king. Do whatever is good in your sight.” Jehu's second letter named the price of that surrender: “If you are on my side, and if you will obey me, then bring the heads of your master’s sons to me at Jezreel by this time tomorrow.” The letter arrived, and the leading men of Samaria slaughtered all seventy and sent the heads in baskets. Jehu ordered them piled in two heaps at the city gate until morning, then stood before the people and placed the act where he wanted it placed, in prophecy: “You are innocent. It was I who conspired against my master and killed him. But who killed all these?” “Know, then, that not a word the LORD has spoken against the house of Ahab will fail, for the LORD has done what He promised through His servant Elijah.” He finished the work at Jezreel himself, killing everyone who remained of Ahab's house there, his great men, his close friends, his priests, without a survivor.

On the road to Samaria the purge widened past its commission. At Beth-eked of the Shepherds, Jehu met forty-two relatives of Ahaziah of Judah, traveling innocently to pay a family visit: “We are relatives of Ahaziah,” they answered, “we have come down to greet the sons of the king and of the queen mother.” They had not heard that the sons of the king and the queen mother were dead. Jehu's order was: “Take them alive.” His men took them alive, then slaughtered them at the well, all forty-two, sparing none. Judah's royal family was now bleeding for a visit made in ignorance. Then Jehu picked up Jehonadab son of Rechab, a man of famous severity, with a handshake test: “Is your heart as true to mine as my heart is to yours?” “Come with me and see my zeal for the LORD!” At Samaria the zeal finished Ahab's house there, and then turned to Ahab's god. Jehu announced a great sacrifice to Baal, greater than Ahab's: “Ahab served Baal a little, but Jehu will serve him a lot.” Every prophet, servant, and priest of Baal in Israel was summoned on pain of death: “Whoever is missing will not live.” The temple filled from end to end, because Jehu was acting deceptively, building a trap out of their own festival. He verified the congregation held none but Baal's own: “Look around to see that there are no servants of the LORD here among you”, “only servants of Baal.” Then he stationed eighty men outside with their lives pledged against a single escape, let the sacrifice begin, and gave the order: “Go in and kill them. Do not let anyone out.” The sacred pillar was dragged out and burned, the temple torn down, and the book records its final use with relish: “they tore down the temple of Baal and made it into a latrine, which it is to this day.” “Thus Jehu eradicated Baal from Israel,” the record says, and keeps going in the same breath.

Then the book delivers its double verdict on the purger, and both halves stand. The word of the LORD came to Jehu with a dynasty: “Because you have done well in carrying out what is right in My sight and have done to the house of Ahab all that was in My heart, four generations of your sons will sit on the throne of Israel.” And in the next breath: “Yet Jehu was not careful to follow the instruction of the LORD, the God of Israel, with all his heart.” He kept the golden calves at Bethel and Dan, Jeroboam's sin, untouched. The zeal had a border, and the border was everything in Israel's worship that did not belong to Ahab. Already in his reign the LORD began to cut Israel down to size, and Hazael of Aram struck the whole territory east of the Jordan. Jehu reigned twenty-eight years and died, and the dynasty promised him began its four generations with the land already shrinking.

While Samaria was being purged, Ahab's bloodline in Jerusalem tried to finish David's. Athaliah, Ahaziah's mother, Ahab's daughter, saw her son dead and moved to annihilate every royal heir of Judah, so the throne would have no claimant but her. She nearly succeeded. One child was stolen out of the killing: Joash, Ahaziah's infant son, taken by his aunt Jehosheba, a king's daughter married to the high priest, and hidden with his nurse in a bedroom, then in the house of the LORD, for six years, while Athaliah ruled the land. In the seventh year, Jehoiada the priest staged the counter-coup with temple guards, David's own spears and shields from the sanctuary, and a ring of armed men around a seven-year-old. He brought the boy out, set the crown on him, gave him the Testimony, and anointed him, and the people clapped and cried: “Long live the king!” Athaliah heard the trumpets, came into the temple court, saw the king standing by the pillar with the land rejoicing around him, tore her clothes, and screamed: “Treason! Treason!” Jehoiada had her taken out between the ranks and killed at the horses' entrance, because, he had said, “She must not be put to death in the house of the LORD.” The people then tore down Jerusalem's temple of Baal and killed its priest, Jehoiada bound king and people in covenant to be the LORD's people, and the child was seated on the throne while, the book says, “the city was quiet, because Athaliah had been put to the sword at the royal palace.” The lamp promised to David had survived its closest call in a bedroom and a temple storeroom: “Joash was seven years old when he became king.”

title: The Temple Repaired, and Elisha's Last Arrow
subtitle: 2 Kings 12
description: Joash repairs the temple, Israel dwindles under Hazael, and Elisha's last arrow sets a king's limit.
paragraphs: The hidden child grew up to be a temple builder, with a qualifier the book attaches to his whole reign: “Joash did what was right in the eyes of the LORD all the days he was instructed by Jehoiada the priest.” All the days of the instruction, not longer. Even so, “the high places were not removed; the people continued sacrificing and burning incense there.” Joash's great work was the repair of the house his great-grandfather's generation had let decay and Athaliah's sons had plundered. His first system failed: the priests collected the sacred money for twenty-three years and the damage went unrepaired. The king confronted them, “Why have you not repaired the damage to the temple?” and built a simpler machine, a chest with a hole bored in its lid beside the altar, the money counted by the royal scribe and the high priest together, and paid straight to the workmen, the carpenters, builders, masons, and stonecutters. The book pauses on the honesty of the arrangement with a sentence any treasurer would envy: “No accounting was required from the men who received the money to pay the workmen, because they acted with integrity.” The repaired temple outlasted its repairer. When Hazael of Aram took Gath and turned toward Jerusalem, Joash bought him off with the temple's dedicated gold, his fathers' and his own, and Hazael withdrew. The boy Jehoiada had crowned was assassinated by his own servants at Beth-millo, and his son Amaziah took the throne.

In the north, Jehu's son Jehoahaz inherited a kingdom being ground down by that same Hazael, until his army was a remnant the text counts like small change: “Jehoahaz had no army left, except fifty horsemen, ten chariots, and ten thousand foot soldiers”, because Aram “had destroyed them and made them like the dust at threshing.” Jehoahaz sought the favor of the LORD, “and the LORD listened to him because He saw the oppression that the king of Aram had inflicted on Israel.” “So the LORD gave Israel a deliverer, and they escaped the power of the Arameans.” The deliverer is never named, and the relief did not reform the relieved: the Asherah pole still stood in Samaria. Jehoash, his son, reigned next, an evil king in the book's verdict, and it is his reign that carries the series' anchor to his deathbed.

Elisha's last scene mirrors his first. When the prophet lay sick with the illness from which he would die, King Jehoash came down to him and wept over him with the exact words Elisha had cried at Elijah's departure: “My father, my father, the chariots and horsemen of Israel!” Elisha's dying act was a piece of prophetic theater. He had the king take a bow, put his own hands over the king's hands on it, and shoot out the east window toward Aram, declaring: “This is the LORD’s arrow of victory, the arrow of victory over Aram, for you shall strike the Arameans in Aphek until you have put an end to them.” Then he told the king to take the arrows and strike the ground. The king struck three times and stopped, politely, moderately, the way kings do. The dying prophet's anger is the last emotion of his ministry: “You should have struck the ground five or six times. Then you would have struck down Aram until you had put an end to it. But now you will strike down Aram only three times.” The measure of the victory had been set by the measure of the striking, and Jehoash had rationed his own deliverance. Elisha died and was buried, and even his grave would not stay out of the work: a burial party, surprised by Moabite raiders, threw their dead man into Elisha's tomb in their hurry, and “as soon as his body touched the bones of Elisha, the man was revived and stood up on his feet.”

Jehoash went on to defeat Ben-hadad three times and recover the cities Hazael had taken, three victories, exactly the number of the arrows, no more. The chapter frames those years with a sentence that explains the whole era of the book, why a kingdom this faithless was still standing at all: “the LORD was gracious to Israel and had compassion on them”, “because of His covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.” “And to this day, the LORD has been unwilling to destroy them or cast them from His presence.” The anchor of the series so far is buried. From here the narrator carries the kings alone, and the road turns down.

title: The Quick Kings and the Foreign Altar
subtitle: 2 Kings 14
description: Amaziah's pride, Jeroboam's prosperity, a line of murdered kings, and Ahaz's foreign altar.
paragraphs: From here the book changes pace, and the change is the message: reigns that once filled chapters now get paragraphs, because there is less and less left to say. Judah first. Amaziah, Joash's son, “did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, but not as his father David had done”, and the grading itself has become a sliding scale. His reign holds one act of law worth pausing on. He executed his father's assassins but spared their sons, obeying the written limit: “Fathers must not be put to death for their children, and children must not be put to death for their fathers; each is to die for his own sin.” Then he beat Edom in the Valley of Salt, and the victory swelled him into challenging Israel: “Come, let us meet face to face,” he said. Jehoash of Israel answered with a fable sharp enough to be quoted whole: a thistle in Lebanon proposed marriage to a cedar, and a wild beast trampled the thistle. The moral he drew for Amaziah was plain: “You have indeed defeated Edom, and your heart has become proud. Glory in that and stay at home.” “Why should you stir up trouble so that you fall”, you and Judah with you? Amaziah would not listen. Judah was routed at Beth-shemesh, Amaziah was captured, and Jehoash broke down four hundred cubits of Jerusalem's wall and emptied the temple and palace treasuries. The king who had spared the assassins' sons outlived his conqueror by fifteen years and was himself killed by conspirators at Lachish.

Israel, meanwhile, had its longest and most prosperous reign of the whole sad sequence, and the book refuses to call it a success. Jeroboam, Jehoash's son, reigned forty-one years in Samaria, did evil like every king before him, and under him the borders swelled back to their Solomonic reach, from Lebo-hamath to the Sea of the Arabah. It happened, the text says, “according to the word that the LORD, the God of Israel, had spoken through His servant Jonah son of Amittai, the prophet from Gath-hepher.” Jonah's own book waits ahead in this series, in the prophets' run; here he is one line of credit in a king's record. The reason for the prosperity is given, and it is not the king: “the LORD saw that the affliction of the Israelites, both slave and free, was very bitter. There was no one to help Israel”, and He had not said He would blot out Israel's name, “He would not blot out the name of Israel from under heaven”, so He saved them by the hand of Jeroboam. Deliverance as an act of memory, delivered through a king who learned nothing from it.

When Jeroboam died, the north fell apart at the speed of its own violence. His son Zechariah reigned six months and was struck down in front of the people by Shallum, and with him ended the house of Jehu, at exactly the length the LORD had promised it: “Four generations of your sons will sit on the throne of Israel.” Shallum reigned one month before Menahem killed him, and Menahem announced his reign at Tiphsah, a town that would not open its gates: “he attacked Tiphsah and ripped open all the pregnant women.” The atrocity Elisha had wept over in Hazael now had an Israelite author. In Menahem's reign the shadow that will swallow the book first touched the land: Pul, king of Assyria, invaded, and Menahem bought him off with a thousand talents of silver taxed at fifty shekels from every wealthy man in Israel. Pekahiah followed his father for two years and was murdered by his own officer Pekah, and in Pekah's days the Assyrian came back as Tiglath-pileser and stopped accepting money. He took Ijon, Abel-beth-maacah, Janoah, Kedesh, Hazor, Gilead, and Galilee, all the land of Naphtali, “and he took the people as captives to Assyria.” The first deportation, a whole region carried off, and Hoshea closed the sequence by murdering Pekah. Six kings in this episode's Israel thread, four of them by assassination.

Judah's thread runs slower and in some ways worse. Azariah reigned fifty-two years in Jerusalem, did right, kept the high places, and spent his reign a leper in a separate house, “the LORD afflicted the king with leprosy until the day he died”, while his son Jotham governed. Jotham did right too, and rebuilt the Upper Gate of the temple. Then came Ahaz, and the book's verdict drops the sliding scale entirely: unlike David, he did not do right. “he walked in the ways of the kings of Israel and even sacrificed his son in the fire”, and “he sacrificed and burned incense on the high places, on the hills, and under every green tree.” Besieged by Aram and Israel together, Ahaz did what Menahem had done, at a higher price and in fuller submission. His message to Tiglath-pileser is the most abject sentence any king of Judah speaks in the book: “I am your servant and your son. Come up and save me from the hands of the kings of Aram and Israel, who are rising up against me.” Assyria came, destroyed Damascus, killed Rezin, and Ahaz went up to meet his rescuer in the conquered city, where he saw an altar he admired. He sent its measurements and plans home to Uriah the priest, who built the copy before the king returned. Ahaz offered on the new altar, moved the bronze altar of the LORD to its north side, demoted to a private oracle, and gave the order that defines his reign: “But I will use the bronze altar to seek guidance.” Then, on account of the king of Assyria, he cut up the temple's bronze stands, took the great Sea down off its oxen, removed the Sabbath canopy, and closed the royal entrance. Solomon's house was being dismantled piece by piece by David's own heir, as tribute furniture for a foreign throne. And Ahaz rested with his fathers, and his son Hezekiah reigned in his place, the book's next great surprise waiting in a single sentence.

title: Samaria Falls
subtitle: 2 Kings 17
description: Samaria falls after three years of siege, and the book reads out the verdict it has compiled for centuries.
paragraphs: Hoshea, who took the throne by murdering Pekah, was Israel's last king, and the book's faint grading follows him to the end: “he did evil in the sight of the LORD, but not like the kings of Israel who preceded him.” He began as Assyria's vassal, paying tribute to Shalmaneser, and then conspired, sending envoys to King So of Egypt and withholding the tribute. The Assyrian king arrested him, chained him in prison, and invaded the whole land, and Samaria held out under siege for three years. In Hoshea's ninth year the city fell, and the deportation made permanent what the raids of the last episode had begun: “the king of Assyria captured Samaria and carried away the Israelites to Assyria, where he settled them in Halah, in Gozan by the Habor River, and in the cities of the Medes.” The northern kingdom, ten tribes, two hundred years of kings from Jeroboam to Hoshea, ends in a sentence of geography: Halah, Gozan, the cities of the Medes, places the book's first readers could not have found on a map.

Then the narrator stops telling the story and renders the verdict, in the longest sustained sermon in the books of Kings, and this episode carries it as the text gives it, unsoftened. It opens with the whole explanation in one sentence: “All this happened because the people of Israel had sinned against the LORD their God, who had brought them out of the land of Egypt from under the hand of Pharaoh king of Egypt.” What follows is the catalogue the story has been compiling since the first calf. They built high places everywhere, “From watchtower to fortified city, they built high places in all their cities”, set up sacred pillars and Asherah poles “on every high hill and under every green tree”, and served idols under the one flat prohibition: “You shall not do this thing.” They did some of it in secret: “The Israelites secretly did things against the LORD their God that were not right.” And the warning system had run for centuries, through every prophet and seer, with one message: “Turn from your wicked ways and keep My commandments and statutes, according to the entire Law that I commanded your fathers and delivered to you through My servants the prophets.” “But they would not listen, and they stiffened their necks like their fathers, who did not believe the LORD their God.” The sermon's most quoted line is its coldest piece of logic: “They pursued worthless idols and became worthless themselves”. Then the full inventory lands at once: “They abandoned all the commandments of the LORD their God and made for themselves two cast idols of calves and an Asherah pole. They bowed down to all the host of heaven and served Baal.” “They sacrificed their sons and daughters in the fire and practiced divination and soothsaying.” “They devoted themselves to doing evil in the sight of the LORD”, provoking Him to anger.

The verdict follows the catalogue the way sentence follows evidence: “So the LORD was very angry with Israel, and He removed them from His presence. Only the tribe of Judah remained”, and the sermon refuses to let the surviving kingdom stand outside the dock: “even Judah did not keep the commandments of the LORD their God, but lived according to the customs Israel had introduced.” The thread that began at Shechem is gathered up by name: Jeroboam “led Israel away from following the LORD and caused them to commit a great sin”, and Israel persisted in it to the end. “Finally, the LORD removed Israel from His presence, as He had declared through all His servants the prophets. So Israel was exiled from their homeland into Assyria, where they are to this day.” The phrase matters: to this day. The book is written from the far side of the exile it is describing, and its verdict was still standing when it was written.

The chapter ends in the emptied land, with its new tenants. The king of Assyria settled peoples from Babylon, Cuthah, Avva, Hamath, and Sepharvaim in Samaria's towns, and when lions began killing the settlers, the diagnosis sent to Assyria was theological: “The peoples that you have removed and placed in the cities of Samaria do not know the requirements of the God of the land.” So one of the exiled Israelite priests was sent back to live at Bethel, of all places, Jeroboam's own shrine, to teach the newcomers how to worship the LORD. What he taught landed in soil already planted. Each nation made its own gods and set them in the shrines on the high places, Babylon's Succoth-benoth, Cuth's Nergal, Hamath's Ashima, the Avvites' Nibhaz and Tartak, and the Sepharvites burning their children to Adrammelech and Anammelech. The book's refrain for the mixture is repeated until it becomes the region's permanent description: “They worshiped the LORD, but they also served their own gods”. “To this day they are still practicing their former customs.” And the last word on the northern land belongs to the children: “So these nations worshiped the LORD but also served their idols, and to this day their children and grandchildren continue to do as their fathers did.” The kingdom of Israel is gone from the story. Judah remains, alone, with Assyria camped permanently in the world's future and a sermon now on record that has already told the reader exactly how a kingdom like this ends.

title: Hezekiah and the Assyrian
subtitle: 2 Kings 18
description: Hezekiah breaks Assyria's script with silence, sackcloth, and a letter spread before the LORD.
paragraphs: After Ahaz comes the book's highest verdict on any king of Judah: Hezekiah “did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, just as his father David had done.” Not the sliding scale of his ancestors, the David grade itself. He removed the high places his righteous predecessors had all left standing, shattered the sacred pillars, cut down the Asherah poles, and demolished even the bronze snake Moses had made, because Israel had begun burning incense to it: “He also demolished the bronze snake called Nehushtan that Moses had made, for up to that time the Israelites had burned incense to it.” The book's summary is unmatched on either throne: “Hezekiah trusted in the LORD, the God of Israel. No king of Judah was like him, either before him or after him.” “And the LORD was with Hezekiah, and he prospered wherever he went. He rebelled against the king of Assyria and refused to serve him.” The rebellion is where the episode's trouble starts. Samaria fell in his sixth year, on schedule, and in his fourteenth year Sennacherib of Assyria took every fortified city of Judah. Hezekiah first tried his father's tool: “I have done wrong; withdraw from me, and I will pay whatever you demand from me.” The price was three hundred talents of silver and thirty of gold, and to pay it Hezekiah emptied the temple treasury and stripped the gold from the temple doors he himself had plated. The tribute changed nothing. Assyria sent its three great officers with a great army anyway, and they took their stand by the aqueduct of the upper pool, where the city's officials came out to negotiate and the whole population could listen from the wall.

The speech the Rabshakeh delivered there is the finest piece of enemy rhetoric in the Bible, and the book gives it in full. He opened by stripping Hezekiah's strategy to a slogan: “You claim to have a strategy and strength for war, but these are empty words. In whom are you now trusting, that you have rebelled against me?” Egypt was a splintered reed “that will pierce the hand of anyone who leans on it”. And he had a theological argument built for the wall's defenders: “is He not the One whose high places and altars Hezekiah has removed”, this God they claimed to trust? He mocked the army with a wager, two thousand horses if Judah could find riders for them, and then played his strongest card, that Assyria's invasion was itself commissioned: “The LORD Himself said to me”, and the inner word he claimed was, “Go up against this land and destroy it.” The officials begged him to switch to Aramaic, the language of diplomacy, out of the people's hearing. He refused and answered in Hebrew, louder, addressing the men on the wall over the officials' heads, and describing what siege does to a city in terms too coarse to soften. Then came the offer, pitched like a travel brochure over a starving wall: “Do not let Hezekiah deceive you; he cannot deliver you from my hand.” “Make peace with me and come out to me. Then every one of you will eat from his own vine and his own fig tree and drink water from his own cistern”, until deportation to “a land of grain and new wine, a land of bread and vineyards, a land of olive trees and honey”. And the close was the catalogue of the fallen: “Has the god of any nation ever delivered his land from the hand of the king of Assyria?” “Who among all the gods of these lands has delivered his land from my hand? How then can the LORD deliver Jerusalem from my hand?” Against all of it, the city's answer was discipline: “the people remained silent and did not answer a word”, because the king had commanded, “Do not answer him.”

Hezekiah tore his clothes, put on sackcloth, and went into the house of the LORD, and sent his officials, also in sackcloth, to Isaiah son of Amoz. Isaiah appears in this series here, in place, as the book places him; his own book comes at its slot in the prophets' run, and his account of these same days will stand beside this one then, whole and unstitched. Hezekiah's message to him was a birth metaphor for a nation out of strength: “Today is a day of distress, rebuke, and disgrace; for children have come to the point of birth, but there is no strength to deliver them.” “Therefore lift up a prayer for the remnant that still survives.” Isaiah's first answer was short and total: “Do not be afraid of the words you have heard, with which the servants of the king of Assyria have blasphemed Me.” “I will put a spirit in him so that he will hear a rumor and return to his own land, where I will cause him to fall by the sword.” The rumor arrived, Tirhakah of Cush marching out, and Sennacherib withdrew to meet it, but first sent a letter to finish what the Rabshakeh had started: “Do not let your God, in whom you trust, deceive you by saying that Jerusalem will not be delivered into the hand of the king of Assyria.” Hezekiah took the letter up to the house of the LORD and spread it out before Him, an exhibit laid on the courtroom floor, and prayed the prayer the episode is remembered by: “O LORD, God of Israel, enthroned between the cherubim, You alone are God over all the kingdoms of the earth. You made the heavens and the earth.” “Incline Your ear, O LORD, and hear; open Your eyes, O LORD, and see. Listen to the words that Sennacherib has sent to defy the living God.” He conceded the Assyrian record in full, the nations wasted, their gods burned, “for they were not gods, but only wood and stone”, and drew the line at exactly that point: “And now, O LORD our God, please save us from his hand, so that all the kingdoms of the earth may know that You alone, O LORD, are God.”

The answer came through Isaiah with a verdict attached: “I have heard your prayer concerning Sennacherib king of Assyria.” The oracle that followed addressed the Assyrian's boasting as a charge sheet: “Whom have you taunted and blasphemed? Against whom have you raised your voice and lifted your eyes in pride? Against the Holy One of Israel!” The sentence was a herdsman's image for the king of the world: “Because your rage and arrogance against Me have reached My ears, I will put My hook in your nose and My bit in your mouth; I will send you back the way you came.” And the military promise was absolute: “He will not enter this city or shoot an arrow into it. He will not come before it with a shield or build up a siege ramp against it.” “I will defend this city and save it for My own sake and for the sake of My servant David.” That night the promise kept itself: “that very night the angel of the LORD went out and struck down 185,000 men in the camp of the Assyrians.” Sennacherib broke camp, went home to Nineveh, and stayed there, and the book ends his story in the temple of his god Nisroch, where his own sons Adrammelech and Sharezer put him to the sword as he worshiped. The god whose name had headed the Rabshakeh's catalogue of the unconquered could not keep his own king alive in his own house. Jerusalem, which had not fired an arrow, was still standing.

title: Hezekiah's Last Years, and Manasseh
subtitle: 2 Kings 20
description: Hezekiah gains fifteen years and shows Babylon everything; Manasseh spends fifty-five undoing him.
paragraphs: The deliverance of Jerusalem was followed by a death sentence delivered to one man. Hezekiah fell mortally ill, and Isaiah came with a word as blunt as the Rabshakeh's: “Put your house in order, for you are about to die; you will not recover.” The king turned his face to the wall and prayed, and the prayer is a righteous man's whole defense, offered in tears: “Please, O LORD, remember how I have walked before You faithfully and with wholehearted devotion; I have done what is good in Your sight.” Before Isaiah had crossed the middle courtyard on his way out, the word came back reversed: “I have heard your prayer; I have seen your tears. I will surely heal you.” “I will add fifteen years to your life”, and the city would be defended with it. A poultice of figs was laid on the boil, and Hezekiah recovered, and for a sign he was offered the shadow on the stairway of Ahaz moving either way. He chose the harder direction, ruling that lengthening was easy: “It is easy for the shadow to lengthen ten steps”, “but not for it to go back ten steps.” The shadow went back. The man who had spread a letter before the LORD and watched an empire's army die in the night now had fifteen added years, a sign read on a staircase, and a future he had not asked about.

The future arrived as a diplomatic courtesy. Babylon, then a junior power courting allies against Assyria, sent letters and a gift to the recovering king, and Hezekiah received the envoys and showed them everything: the silver, the gold, the spices, the precious oil, the armory, all the storehouses. The book measures the thoroughness with a comprehensive negative: “There was nothing in his palace or in all his dominion that Hezekiah did not show them.” Isaiah came afterward with an audit in three questions. Where did the men come from? “They came from a distant land”, “from Babylon.” What have they seen? “They have seen everything in my palace,” answered Hezekiah. “There is nothing among my treasures that I did not show them.” Then the prophet delivered the word that reaches past Hezekiah's fifteen years to the end of the book itself: “The time will surely come when everything in your palace and all that your fathers have stored up until this day will be carried off to Babylon. Nothing will be left, says the LORD.” “And some of your descendants, your own flesh and blood, will be taken away to be eunuchs in the palace of the king of Babylon.” Hezekiah's response is the most quietly damning line ever given to a good king: “The word of the LORD that you have spoken is good.” The text opens his reasoning to the reader: “Will there not at least be peace and security in my lifetime?” The man who had prayed for the remnant and spread the letter for the city accepted, as good news, a catastrophe scheduled safely beyond his own death. He died honored, remembered for his might and for the pool and tunnel he built to bring water into the city, works of the siege years. His son Manasseh reigned in his place. Manasseh was twelve years old, and some of what Babylon's envoys had admired was still in the storehouses.

Manasseh reigned fifty-five years, the longest reign in the book, and the book treats its length as an indictment rather than a blessing, because he spent it systematically reversing his father. “he rebuilt the high places that his father Hezekiah had destroyed, and he raised up altars for Baal.” “He made an Asherah pole, as King Ahab of Israel had done, and he worshiped and served all the host of heaven.” He built altars to the host of heaven in both courtyards of the house of the LORD itself, the house of which God had said, “In Jerusalem I will put My Name”, and set the carved Asherah pole up inside the temple. “He sacrificed his own son in the fire, practiced sorcery and divination, and consulted mediums and spiritists. He did great evil in the sight of the LORD, provoking Him to anger.” Hezekiah had wept and been heard; his son filled the fifty-five years with everything his father's reform had torn down, replanted in the temple courts. And the people followed where he led: “the people did not listen and Manasseh led them astray, so that they did greater evil than the nations that the LORD had destroyed before the Israelites.” The comparison is the verdict's floor: worse than the nations dispossessed for exactly these practices.

So the prophets brought the sentence, and it reaches back to the last episode's verdict and applies it to the south: “Since Manasseh king of Judah has committed all these abominations, acting more wickedly than the Amorites who preceded him”, “Behold, I am bringing such calamity upon Jerusalem and Judah that the news will reverberate in the ears of all who hear it.” The instruments named for the measuring are borrowed from the north's autopsy: “I will stretch out over Jerusalem the measuring line used against Samaria and the plumb line used against the house of Ahab”, “and I will wipe out Jerusalem as one wipes out a bowl”, “wiping it and turning it upside down.” “So I will forsake the remnant of My inheritance and deliver them into the hands of their enemies.” The book adds its final count against him in a single sentence of scale: “Manasseh shed so much innocent blood that he filled Jerusalem from end to end”. Kings records no repentance for him, not in fifty-five years; Chronicles, when this series reaches it, tells something more of Manasseh, and it will be told there, in its place, whole and unstitched. Manasseh died and was buried in his palace garden. His son Amon copied him for two years, “He abandoned the LORD, the God of his fathers, and did not walk in the way of the LORD”, and was murdered by his own servants. The people of the land executed the conspirators and made Amon's son king in his place. The boy's name was Josiah, and he was eight years old, and everything now depends on what a child raised in Manasseh's palace will do with a throne.

title: Josiah and the Book Found
subtitle: 2 Kings 22
description: A lost book is found in the temple, and Josiah's reform runs back through three centuries of altars.
paragraphs: Josiah became king at eight, in the wreckage of Manasseh's palace, and the book's verdict on him reaches back past every king since David for its comparison: “he did what was right in the eyes of the LORD and walked in all the ways of his father David; he did not turn aside to the right or to the left.” In the eighteenth year of his reign he sent Shaphan the scribe to the temple to fund repairs, with the same trust his ancestor Joash's chest had embodied: “they need not account for the money put into their hands, since they work with integrity.” Then Hilkiah the high priest made the announcement that turns the whole book: “I have found the Book of the Law in the house of the LORD!” A book of God's law, lost inside God's house, through the reigns of kings who sacrificed in its courtyards. Shaphan read it, carried it to the king, reported the repair money first, and then read the book aloud in the king's presence. When Josiah heard the words, he tore his clothes, the gesture this book has used for guilt and grief from Ahaziah's messengers onward, and his command shows he had understood exactly what he had heard: “Go and inquire of the LORD for me, for the people, and for all Judah concerning the words in this book that has been found. For great is the wrath of the LORD that burns against us because our fathers have not obeyed the words of this book by doing all that is written about us.” He did not ask whether the book was authentic. He asked what its wrath meant for a nation that had been breaking it unread for generations.

The delegation went to Huldah the prophetess, in Jerusalem's Second District, and her answer came in two parts, doom and exception, and neither part bends. The doom confirms Manasseh's sentence without revising a word of it: “I am about to bring calamity on this place and on its people, according to all the words of the book that the king of Judah has read”, “because they have forsaken Me and burned incense to other gods, that they might provoke Me to anger with all the works of their hands. My wrath will be kindled against this place and will not be quenched.” The exception is personal, and it is earned by exactly one thing, the king's response to the reading: “because your heart was tender and you humbled yourself before the LORD when you heard what I spoke against this place and against its people, that they would become a desolation and a curse, and because you have torn your clothes and wept before Me, I have heard you”. “Therefore I will indeed gather you to your fathers, and you will be gathered to your grave in peace. Your eyes will not see all the calamity that I will bring on this place.” Josiah is promised the only mercy left in the book: he will not have to watch it.

What he did with a reprieve for himself and none for his nation is the greatest reform in the books of Kings. He gathered all Judah, small and great, read the whole Book of the Covenant aloud in their hearing, stood by the pillar, and covenanted the nation back to its God. Then he cleaned, and the cleaning is told as a catalogue that runs backward through the entire series. Out of the temple came every article made for Baal, Asherah, and the host of heaven, burned in the Kidron fields and their ashes carried to Bethel. The Asherah pole his grandfather had set in the house was ground to powder and its dust thrown on common graves. The idolatrous priests were deposed, the shrine prostitutes' quarters in the temple torn down, Topheth in the Valley of Ben-hinnom desecrated “so that no one could sacrifice his son or daughter in the fire to Molech”, the horses dedicated to the sun removed and their chariots burned, Manasseh's courtyard altars and Ahaz's roof altars pulverized. He went further back than his own dynasty: east of Jerusalem he desecrated the high places Solomon himself had built, for “Ashtoreth the abomination of the Sidonians”, for Chemosh, for Milcom, shrines that had stood for three centuries under every reforming king untouched. And at Bethel he tore down “the altar at Bethel, the high place set up by Jeroboam son of Nebat, who had caused Israel to sin”, ground it to powder, and burned human bones on it to defile it, and in doing so fulfilled, act for act, the prophecy an unnamed man of God had cried against that altar in the days of Jeroboam himself, in the sixth episode of 1 Kings, three hundred years before. Josiah, turning, noticed a tomb and asked, “What is this monument I see?” It was the man of God's own grave. His order was immediate: “Let him rest,” said Josiah. “Do not let anyone disturb his bones.” The reformer spared the bones of the prophet whose words he had just spent a campaign fulfilling.

Then he kept the Passover the book had been waiting centuries to record: “Keep the Passover of the LORD your God, as it is written in this Book of the Covenant.” “No such Passover had been observed from the days of the judges who had governed Israel through all the days of the kings of Israel and Judah.” The verdict follows, the second superlative of the book: “Neither before nor after Josiah was there any king like him, who turned to the LORD with all his heart and with all his soul and with all his strength, according to all the Law of Moses.” Hezekiah trusted like no other; Josiah turned like no other; the book gives each man his own summit and reconciles nothing. And the very next sentence is the coldest in Kings: “Nevertheless, the LORD did not turn away from the fury of His burning anger, which was kindled against Judah because of all that Manasseh had done to provoke Him to anger.” “I will remove Judah from My sight, just as I removed Israel. I will reject this city Jerusalem, which I chose”. The greatest reform in the monarchy's history changed the king's own end and nothing else. The sentence stood.

Josiah died at Megiddo, going out to confront Pharaoh Neco of Egypt, who was marching to the Euphrates to help a dying Assyria, and Neco killed him at the meeting, though the book gives the confrontation three verses and no battle. His servants carried him home, and the people of the land anointed his son Jehoahaz, who reigned three months before Neco imprisoned him at Riblah and hauled him to Egypt to die, taxing Judah a hundred talents of silver and a talent of gold. Neco renamed the next son, Eliakim became Jehoiakim, a king by a foreigner's appointment, paying Egypt's levy by taxing his own people man by man. He did evil, the book says, just as his fathers had done. The reform had lasted exactly one reign, and the reader who has followed the sentence from Manasseh's oracle knows the only question left is the manner and the date. Both arrive in the next episode, and the agent of them is not Egypt.

title: Jerusalem Falls
subtitle: 2 Kings 24
description: Jehoiachin surrenders, Zedekiah is blinded, the temple burns, and the book ends at a Babylonian table.
paragraphs: The last movement of the book opens with the cause stated before the events, in case the reader has forgotten Manasseh's oracle: Babylon came, Jehoiakim served Nebuchadnezzar three years and rebelled, and “the LORD sent Chaldean, Aramean, Moabite, and Ammonite raiders against Jehoiakim in order to destroy Judah, according to the word that the LORD had spoken through His servants the prophets.” “Surely this happened to Judah at the LORD’s command, to remove them from His presence because of the sins of Manasseh and all that he had done”, “and also for the innocent blood he had shed. For he had filled Jerusalem with innocent blood, and the LORD was unwilling to forgive.” Jehoiakim died with Egypt already finished as a power, Babylon holding everything from the Brook of Egypt to the Euphrates. His son Jehoiachin, eighteen years old, reigned three months, and when Nebuchadnezzar came up in person, the young king did the one sensible thing left to a king of Judah: he surrendered, walking out with his mother, his servants, his commanders, and his officials. It saved the city for nine more years and cost everything else. “As the LORD had declared, Nebuchadnezzar also carried off all the treasures from the house of the LORD and the royal palace, and he cut into pieces all the gold articles that Solomon king of Israel had made in the temple of the LORD.” Solomon's gold, cut into pieces: Hezekiah's envoys had once been shown it all. Then the people went: “He carried into exile all Jerusalem”, commanders, mighty men, craftsmen, metalsmiths, “ten thousand captives in all. Only the poorest people of the land remained.” Babylon installed the prisoner's uncle Mattaniah on the emptied throne and renamed him Zedekiah, and the book notes the reason the rest happened with a sentence that removes all suspense: “because of the anger of the LORD, all this happened in Jerusalem and Judah, until He finally banished them from His presence.” Zedekiah, the puppet, also rebelled.

The siege is told in the text's own dates, and this retelling keeps them, because the book wants the arithmetic felt. In Zedekiah's ninth year, on the tenth day of the tenth month, Nebuchadnezzar encamped against Jerusalem and built his siege wall. In the eleventh year, by the ninth day of the fourth month, “the famine in the city was so severe that the people of the land had no food.” That night the city was breached, and the king and his men of war fled through the gate between the two walls by the king's garden, toward the Arabah. The Chaldeans overtook him in the plains of Jericho, where Israel had first entered the land under Joshua, and his army deserted him there. At Riblah they pronounced judgment on the last king of David's line in Jerusalem: “they slaughtered the sons of Zedekiah before his eyes. Then they put out his eyes, bound him with bronze shackles, and took him to Babylon.” The last thing Zedekiah of Judah ever saw was the end of his house.

A month later Nebuzaradan, captain of the guard, came to finish the city. “He burned down the house of the LORD, the royal palace, and all the houses of Jerusalem”, every significant building. The walls were broken down all around. The people who remained were carried into exile, the poorest left behind again to tend vineyards and fields that no longer had owners. And the bronze went the way the gold had gone, in pieces: “the Chaldeans broke up the bronze pillars and stands and the bronze Sea in the house of the LORD, and they carried the bronze to Babylon.” The book lingers over the inventory of Solomon's work one last time, the two pillars, the Sea, the stands, and weighs it in a phrase: “the weight of the bronze from all these articles was beyond measure.” The chief priest Seraiah, the second priest Zephaniah, the doorkeepers, the officials and advisors and sixty men of the city were taken to Riblah and executed there. “So Judah was taken into exile, away from its own land.” The sentence the prophets had been pronouncing since Manasseh, the sentence Samaria had already served, is complete in one line.

What remained in the land got one brief chapter of almost-government. Gedaliah, son of Ahikam, of the family of Shaphan the scribe who had once carried the found Book to Josiah, was made governor at Mizpah, and he swore an oath to the army commanders who came in from the hills: “Do not be afraid of the servants of the Chaldeans. Live in the land and serve the king of Babylon, and it will be well with you.” In the seventh month, Ishmael of the royal family came with ten men and murdered him, along with the Judeans and Chaldeans with him, and the whole remnant, small and great, fled to Egypt for fear of Babylon's answer. The land of Judah was finally empty of everything, king, temple, priesthood, governor, and people, and the book could have ended there, in Egypt, with the flight.

It does not. The last scene is set thirty-seven years into Jehoiachin's exile, in Babylon, in the year a new king, Evil-merodach, took the throne, and “he released King Jehoiachin of Judah from prison.” “And he spoke kindly to Jehoiachin and set his throne above the thrones of the other kings who were with him in Babylon.” The captive who had surrendered at eighteen changed out of his prison clothes, “and he dined regularly at the king’s table for the rest of his life.” The book of Kings, which began with an old king dying in Jerusalem and a son securing a throne, ends with a dethroned king eating at a foreign table on a daily allowance: “the king provided Jehoiachin a daily portion for the rest of his life.” No explanation is attached. No return is promised in these pages, no Cyrus named, no future sketched. The line of David is alive, fed, and seated above the other captive kings in the capital of the empire that destroyed his city, and there the book stops, and this series will leave it exactly there until Chronicles takes up the story from the exile's side, looking back.
